opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the choice wasn't about picking our four "best" models. It was about picking four pieces that together form a usable stack for embodied intelligence.

In robotics, what holds the field back usually isn't one missing model. It's that the pieces don't connect. One group has good perception, another has a policy model, a third has a simulator, and none of them talk to each other. So we asked: if a university lab or a small startup picked up our release, could they actually build something end to end? That's why the four cover different layers. One is about understanding the physical world, especially spatial and 3D perception, because a robot that can't reliably tell where things are can't do anything downstream. One is closer to a world model, predicting how the scene evolves when the robot acts, which matters a lot for data efficiency. One sits at the action level, mapping perception and instructions to motor behavior. The fourth is more infrastructure: the glue that makes training and evaluation reproducible.

Timing was the second reason. Early 2026 felt like a window. The community was converging on some shared ideas about vision-language-action models and world models, but there wasn't yet a strong, open, well-documented baseline that people trusted. If you release when everyone is still guessing, you can help set the standard. If you wait a year, you're just one more checkpoint.

The third reason is more personal. I come from computer vision and generative modeling, and I saw how much open source accelerated those fields. Image generation moved incredibly fast once strong open models existed, because thousands of people could poke at them, find failure cases, and build on them. Robotics is far more fragmented because of hardware differences, so I think openness matters even more there. Closed models in robotics tend to overfit to one company's robots and one company's data.

To be candid, we also held things back. Some models weren't mature enough, and releasing something half-baked in robotics can waste a lot of people's time, since experiments on real hardware are expensive. So the bar was: is it solid enough that someone else can reproduce our results and build on it? These four met that bar.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the honest answer is that we didn't start from "which four should we open source." We started from the question of what a robot actually needs in order to act in the world, and once you lay that out, the four pieces fall out almost naturally.

A robot has to see, so there's a perception model. It has to understand where things are in three-dimensional space, not just recognize them in a flat image, so there's a spatial understanding model. It has to connect what it sees to what it should do, so there's a vision-language-action model that maps observations and instructions into motor commands. And it has to be able to imagine the consequences of an action before it takes it, so there's a world model that predicts how the scene will evolve. Those four together are, in our view, the minimum closed loop for embodied intelligence. Releasing one of them alone would have been a demo. Releasing all four is a stack someone can actually build on.

The second reason is more about the state of the field. In language, open models forced the whole community to converge on shared benchmarks and shared infrastructure, and progress accelerated. Robotics in early 2026 still felt fragmented. Every lab had its own data format, its own simulator, its own evaluation. We felt that the most useful thing we could do was not to keep a slightly better model behind a wall for six months, but to put out a coherent set of baselines so people stop re-solving the same problems. The value of a foundation model in robotics is overwhelmingly in the data and the ecosystem around it, not in the weights themselves. If we're right about that, then open sourcing is not a sacrifice. It's the strategy.

And the third reason, frankly, is that we wanted feedback at scale. Robots fail in the long tail. You cannot discover the long tail inside one company's lab. The moment the models went out, people were running them on hardware we had never touched, in environments we had never imagined, and sending back failure cases. That's worth more to us than any amount of internal evaluation.

So in short: four models because that's the shape of the problem, open because that's how the field moves faster, and January because we felt the pieces were finally good enough to be useful rather than just interesting.
